lesson.title: Circles and Shading: Graphing Inequalities on a Number Line
lesson.summary: Use open and closed circles together with directional shading on a number line to represent the full, infinite solution set of a linear inequality.
lesson.body:
A linear inequality in one variable typically has infinitely many solutions, so listing them all is impossible, but a number line makes it possible to show every solution at once using a picture instead of a list. The two building blocks of this picture are the circle placed at the boundary value and the shaded arrow that extends from it. Which kind of circle to draw depends directly on the inequality symbol involved, which is why a solid grasp of inequality symbols matters before graphing them.

When the inequality uses strictly less than or strictly greater than, the boundary value itself is not a solution, so it is marked with an open circle, drawn as a small unfilled ring centered on that point of the number line. When the inequality uses less than or equal to or greater than or equal to, the boundary value is included in the solution set, so it is marked with a closed circle, drawn as a small filled in dot. From that circle, an arrow is drawn along the number line in the direction of all the other solutions: to the right for greater than or greater than or equal to, and to the left for less than or less than or equal to, since numbers increase to the right and decrease to the left on a standard number line.

Consider graphing the solution set of x is greater than 2. Because the symbol is strictly greater than, an open circle is placed at 2 on the number line, showing that 2 itself is not a solution. From that open circle, an arrow extends to the right, through 3, 4, 5, and every other number greater than 2, showing that all of those values are solutions. Now consider x is less than or equal to negative 1. Because the symbol includes or equal to, a closed circle is placed at negative 1, showing that negative 1 is included as a solution. From that closed circle, an arrow extends to the left, through negative 2, negative 3, and beyond, since those numbers are also less than negative 1.

Graphing often follows directly after solving an inequality, connecting this section back to the algebra itself. Solve 2x minus 3 is less than or equal to 7 before graphing it. Adding 3 to both sides gives 2x is less than or equal to 10, and dividing both sides by 2 gives x is less than or equal to 5. Since the symbol is less than or equal to, the graph has a closed circle at 5 with an arrow extending to the left, covering 5 and every number smaller than it. Checking a value from inside the shaded region, such as x equals 0, confirms the graph is correct: 2 times 0 minus 3 is negative 3, and negative 3 is indeed less than or equal to 7.

The picture itself is worth reading back into words, since that is ultimately the point of drawing it. A closed circle at 5 with shading toward the left says, in a single image, that 5 is a solution, that every number smaller than 5 is also a solution, and that every number larger than 5 is not. This is a much faster way to communicate an infinite solution set than listing numbers, and it becomes the visual foundation for combining two inequalities on the same number line, which is exactly what happens when compound inequalities joined by and or or are graphed later in this unit.
